body: {"total":8,"records":[{"title":"In-situ simulation for rapid response teams and time to first critical intervention: a before-after study in one hospital","authors":"Lindqvist-Oduya S, Marchetti-Brandt K, Achebe-Nakamura P","year":2018,"venue":"Acute Care Simulation Practice","doi":"10.5555/sace.2018.0114","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One hospital introduced monthly unannounced in-situ simulations for its rapid response team, each followed by a structured debrief. We compared 12 months of real calls before and after the change. The median time from call to first critical intervention fell from 11.2 to 8.4 minutes. Unplanned intensive care admission after a call did not change. The study had no control group, a new early warning score was introduced during the after period, and the team members changed over the two years, so the fall cannot be attributed to simulation alone."},{"title":"A stepped-wedge evaluation of in-situ simulation for medical emergency teams across five hospitals","authors":"Ferreira-Holm D, Okafor-Lindgren T, Sato-Mensah R, Petit-Kowalski A","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Interprofessional Resuscitation Education","doi":"10.5555/jire.2022.0207","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Five hospitals introduced monthly in-situ simulation for medical emergency teams in a random order over 15 months. Across 6,480 real calls, the median time from call to first critical intervention fell by 3.1 minutes after introduction, after adjustment for calendar time. Unplanned intensive care admission within 12 hours of a call did not change (odds ratio 0.96, 95 percent CI 0.81 to 1.14), and death within 24 hours was too rare to compare. Simulations were cancelled in 14 percent of planned months because of staffing. The authors note that five clusters gave imprecise estimates of between-hospital effects."},{"title":"Team performance scores in simulation and performance in real rapid response calls: a validation study","authors":"Kaur-Whitfield M, Varadi-Osei J","year":2020,"venue":"Acute Care Simulation Practice","doi":"10.5555/sace.2020.0048","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared the scores of 38 rapid response teams on a standard simulation checklist with blinded ratings of the same teams in video-recorded real calls. Simulation checklist scores correlated weakly with real-call performance (correlation coefficient 0.21). Time to first critical intervention in simulation correlated better with the same time in real calls than checklist scores did. Teams that scored highly in simulation often lost role clarity in crowded real calls. The authors caution against using simulation checklist scores as the main outcome of team training."},{"title":"Unannounced in-situ simulation on working wards: safety events, cancellations and staff experience","authors":"Mbatha-Rourke L, Castellanos-Iwu H","year":2019,"venue":"Ward Safety Practice Notes","doi":"10.5555/psip.2019.0133","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 212 unannounced in-situ simulations run on medical and surgical wards over three years. Three simulations were interrupted by a real call on the same ward and stopped at once, with no delay to the real call. No patient harm was attributed to a simulation. In a staff questionnaire, 41 percent of ward nurses reported anxiety when an unannounced simulation began, and several were unsure at first whether the event was real. Clear signage, a stop word and advance notice to the ward manager were added after the first year."},{"title":"Debriefing structure and learning in interprofessional simulation: a systematic review","authors":"Harcourt-Adeyemi N, Rasmussen-Tanaka B, Oduya-Grieve C","year":2021,"venue":"Journal of Interprofessional Resuscitation Education","doi":"10.5555/jire.2021.0162","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We included 27 studies of debriefing after interprofessional simulation. Structured debriefing with a trained facilitator was associated with better learning outcomes than unstructured discussion in most comparisons, but outcomes were mostly knowledge and self-rated confidence measured immediately after the session. Only four studies measured behaviour in clinical practice, and none measured patient outcomes. Debriefs longer than 20 minutes were no better than shorter ones. Study quality was low to moderate, and most studies were run in simulation centres rather than on clinical wards, so their relevance to in-situ programmes is uncertain."},{"title":"Families' experience of rapid response calls on general wards","authors":"Achterberg-Lemaire F, Nwosu-Hallberg K","year":2017,"venue":"Family-Centred Acute Care","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke with 18 family members who had been present when a rapid response team was called for a relative on a general ward. Families described confusion about who the arriving clinicians were and what their roles were, being asked to leave without explanation, and a lack of information after the team left. Several families had noticed their relative's deterioration before staff did and did not know how to raise concern. Families valued a named person who explained what was happening. Participants came from two hospitals and were contacted by ward managers."},{"title":"Latent safety threats identified by in-situ simulation on general wards","authors":"Rahman-Holt E, Sorensen-Brennan M","year":2023,"venue":"Ward Safety Practice Notes","doi":"10.5555/psip.2023.0079","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across 146 in-situ simulations on general wards in three hospitals, teams and observers identified a mean of 1.8 latent safety threats per simulation, such as missing airway equipment, wrong suction connectors, blocked bed access and unclear calling procedures. Most threats were fixed within a month. Hospitals that fed threats into a safety tracking system resolved more of them than hospitals that relied on informal follow-up. The study did not measure whether resolving threats changed real-call outcomes, and threats were classified by the simulation faculty without a second rater."},{"title":"Intracluster correlation of rapid response outcomes between hospitals: estimates for planning cluster studies","authors":"Petrov-Amadi J, Lindgren-Castillo R","year":2024,"venue":"Rapid Response Research Methods","doi":"10.5555/rrm.2024.0021","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We estimated intracluster correlation coefficients for rapid response call outcomes from 41,300 calls in 22 hospitals over three years. The coefficient was 0.04 for time from call to first critical intervention, 0.02 for unplanned intensive care admission within 12 hours and 0.01 for death within 24 hours. Coefficients were larger for hospitals of very different size and were stable across years. The authors provide the estimates, with their confidence intervals, for sample size calculations in cluster and stepped-wedge studies of rapid response interventions."}]}
